messages.author: fd404cb3ef2d7513
messages.subject: part-time residency
parts:
Dear community,

I was hoping to get your advice on an approach I have been considering. I have a stationary, automated VHF-grid that tracks bats in a small area of about 25 km2. My goal is to analyze the habitat preferences of bats in this area using rsf. However, I have noticed that some of the bats are not range residents as they escape the VHF-grid on certain nights (but they return after some time).

To address this issue, I plan to conduct a night-specific rsf analysis and exclude any nights where the variograms show non-residency. Afterwards, I would like to average the rsf over all individual nights. However, I am unsure if that is a valid approach - what is your opinion on this?

Thank you in advance and best,

Markus

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: part-time residency
parts:
Hi Markus,

I think generally it makes sense to classify segments of the data by behavior and include those behavioral categories as predictors.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: part-time residency
parts:
Hi Chris,
thanks again for the quick reply. So, I would have two additional questions, if you did not mind.

As you suggested, I would annotate a column to the data where I add the behavioral status of each night.
So in the end, for the rsf, I would have a formula like this for instance:
rsf.fit(data_ID1,UD_ID1,R=list(rastercov),formula=~rastercov:resident+rastercov:nonresident)

I see, that "UD_ID1" has to be different between resident and nonresident nights and need to correspond to the behavioral state. So, I need to calculate an UD for resident and an UD for nonresident nights. But how can I combine them somehow and implement them into the formula above?

Or should I just do separate analyses for residents and nonresidents and do some kind of meta analysis afterwards to compare them?

Best,
Markus
